items.claim: updateAddrs' deferred `ac.transport.GracefulClose()` now runs while ac.mu is still locked, contradicting the comment above it; it only completes because the spawned goroutine later unlocks.
items.consequence: SubConn is READY on an address missing from the new list: updateAddrs returns with ac.mu held, GracefulClose takes t.mu and blocks in onClose on ac.mu until the new goroutine reaches its Unlock. The balancer's UpdateAddresses call and all users of that transport's t.mu stall meanwhile. No deadlock today (focused pickfirst/subconn tests pass), but any future pre-unlock step in resetTransportAndUnlock that needs t.mu or the caller would deadlock.

items.claim: updateAddrs hands a locked ac.mu to a goroutine that has not started (`go ac.resetTransportAndUnlock()`), so the function returns with the mutex held and no owner on the stack.
items.consequence: Maintenance cost: anything added after the `go` statement or in a defer runs under a lock it appears not to hold, and tearDown, getTransport, getReadyTransport and onClose all block until the scheduler runs the new goroutine. A sturdier fix does the Connecting transition (ctx check, backoff/deadline computation, updateConnectivityState) synchronously under the lock in connect/updateAddrs, unlocks there, and spawns only the unlocked tryAllAddrs/backoff part.

items.claim: The race fix ships with no regression test; the only coverage is the incidental xDS Test/AuthorityRevive, which failed about 0.4% of runs before the fix.
items.consequence: A later refactor reintroduces an unlock between connect()'s Idle check and the Connecting transition. Two concurrent Connect() calls again dial twice and orphan a transport, and CI passes about 99.6% of the time. A deterministic test (call Connect() twice concurrently with a counting dialer and assert one dial) would catch it.

items.claim: With an empty address list, updateAddrs sets Idle and then starts resetTransportAndUnlock, which sets Connecting and stays there forever because tryAllAddrs over zero addresses returns nil.
items.consequence: A balancer calls UpdateAddresses(sc, nil) on a CONNECTING or READY SubConn. The balancer sees Idle then Connecting, its Connect() is ignored as non-idle, and no transport or further state change ever arrives, so RPCs on that SubConn hang until Shutdown. This predates the PR but sits in the touched function and is unchanged by it.

items.claim: The new doc comment says resetTransportAndUnlock "unconditionally connects", but it returns without any state transition when ac.ctx is already cancelled.
items.consequence: updateAddrs on a READY SubConn with a wrong address sets ac.transport = nil and recreates ac.ctx from ac.cc.ctx. If the channel context is already cancelled (Close in progress), the goroutine returns here and leaves state READY with a nil transport until tearDown runs. On the connect() path it returns nil with the state still Idle, so callers relying on the documented contract are misled.

items.claim: A cancelled connection attempt is treated as success and resets ac.backoffIdx to 0, because createTransport returns nil when ctx is cancelled.
items.consequence: A SubConn that has failed repeatedly (backoffIdx = 3) is Connecting when updateAddrs cancels the attempt and starts a new goroutine. The old goroutine's dial completes, sees ctx.Err(), closes the transport and returns nil, and the old resetTransportAndUnlock zeroes backoffIdx. Later failures of the new attempt back off from the base delay again, giving more aggressive reconnects than the backoff policy intends. This predates the PR.

items.claim: On tryAllAddrs error, ac.cc.resolveNow is called before checking whether the attempt was merely cancelled.
items.consequence: Every updateAddrs that interrupts a Connecting attempt, and every tearDown during connect, makes the old goroutine get errConnClosing and trigger a spurious name re-resolution. That can produce another address update and another updateAddrs, adding resolver churn. This predates the PR.
